audits.question: Check the entry's Meroitic decipherment-versus-understanding and proposed language-family affiliation distinction using a scholarly passage; sound values are not unrestricted translation or identity with Old Nubian.
audits.entry_locator: corpus/knowledge/civilizations/nubia-kush.md, section 'Language family and writing: what is actually deciphered?', lines 48-52: line 48 'Critical correction ... Griffith established the basic sign readings in the early twentieth century; the language remains incompletely understood. [R12, pp. 3-4]'; line 50 'Affiliation, proposed: Rilly's North Eastern Sudanic analysis relates Meroitic to a grouping including Nubian, Nara, Taman, and Nyima; this is not identity with Old Nubian ... [R12, ch. III]'; line 51 Rowan as competing argument [Ro06]
audits.entry_claim: The entry asserts that Griffith established the basic sign readings in the early twentieth century while the language remains incompletely understood (transliteration without translation), and that Rilly's North Eastern Sudanic analysis relates Meroitic to a grouping including Nubian, Nara, Taman, and Nyima as a proposed affiliation - not identity with Old Nubian or a modern Nubian language - with Rowan's Afroasiatic proposal recorded as a genuine competing argument, not a settled replacement.
audits.source_citation: Claude Rilly, 'Recent Research on Meroitic, the Ancient Language of Sudan', Ityopis 1 (2011), open-access PDF; paper authored by the proposer of the NES grouping
audits.source_locator: Abstract (PDF p. 1) and the NES sub-group statement, PDF p. 6 ('Meroitic belongs to a sub-group of East Sudanic ... comprizing also Nubian ... Nara ... Taman ... and Nyima')
audits.source_excerpt: Meroitic belongs to a sub-group of East Sudanic, which he termed 'Northern East Sudanic' (NES), comprizing also Nubian [...], Nara [...], Taman (a dialectal group from the Chad-Sudan borderland) and Nyima (two languages from the Nuba Mountains in Sudan).
audits.retrieval_method: Direct curl download of the open-access journal PDF over HTTP followed by pdftotext extraction; quotation read from the extracted page text (PDF p. 6). No search-engine mediation; scratch copy kept in reports/supplement-opencode-1/scratch/round6-12/rilly_2011_ityopis.pdf/.txt
audits.basis: The retrieved sentence names the same four branches as entry line 50 (Nubian, Nara, Taman, Nyima) under the same proposed sub-group label, matching the entry's 'proposed' calibration. The same PDF's abstract (p. 1) separately carries the decipherment-versus-understanding distinction: 'The script was deciphered 100 years ago but the knowledge of the language remains scanty because no bilingual texts were found.'
audits.coupling_implication: Sound values/transliteration, semantic understanding, and family affiliation stay three separate layers: a deciphered script does not yield unrestricted translation, and the NES grouping is a proposal that must not be collapsed into 'Meroitic = Old Nubian'. For design coupling this preserves the entry's table (sign recognition -> transliteration -> phonology -> semantics) and keeps borrowed sign shapes with locally reassigned values, rather than letting real-world affiliation questions license word borrowing.
audits.limits: The entry cites R&D 2012 ch. III; the decisive retrieved passage is Rilly's later open-access summary article by the same author, not the book chapter itself, and Rilly writes 'Northern East Sudanic' where the entry writes 'North Eastern Sudanic' (same sub-group, naming variant recorded). Rilly also frames NES as confirmation of Trigger's 1964 East Sudanic assumption - the entry's attribution of the analysis to Rilly matches his own framing ('termed' by him) but the confirmation-not-origin nuance is recorded here. Rowan 2006 full text was NOT retrieved: the CiteSeerX attempt returned an HTML page, not the PDF, so its Afroasiatic argument rests on tertiary confirmation only (see corroboration_rowan_tertiary); the entry itself claims only bibliographic status for it. The Old Nubian non-identity leg rests on the R&D excerpt p. 8 passage in corroboration_old_nubian_passage. All classifications author-side, not independent promotion verification.

audits.question: Check kandake/title translation and royal-woman identification against a text/object or scholarly passage; keep reigning queen, queen mother, royal imagery and universal gender-system claims separate.
audits.entry_locator: corpus/knowledge/civilizations/nubia-kush.md, section 'Kandake: title, translation, and royal-women linguistics', lines 70-88: line 74 table row '`kdke`, conventionally kandake - A Meroitic royal-woman title; "queen" or "queen mother" must be contextualized'; line 76 'Greek/Latin Kandake/Candace forms - Foreign transmission of a title'; line 80 reference anchors [R12, glossary and ruler list] and [T97, pp. 213-214]; line 82 'a written form lacking `n` is not sufficient to pronounce the title without a nasal'; line 83 'Amanirenas and Amanishakheto are named rulers, not variant names of one "Candace"'; lines 85-87 Strabo 17.1.54 report, its attribution, and the calibration bullet
audits.entry_claim: The entry asserts that `kdke`, conventionally kandake, is a Meroitic royal-woman title whose rendering as 'queen' or 'queen mother' must be contextualized; that Greek/Latin Kandake/Candace is foreign transmission of a title, not a reconstruction of Meroitic sounds; that Amanirenas and Amanishakheto are distinct named rulers requiring individual documentation; and that Strabo 17.1.54 reports a ruling 'Candace' with her commanders, a son, embassies, and war with Rome - attributed political evidence, not a survey of Kushite gender relations and not proof of universal female succession or matriarchy.
audits.source_citation: Strabo, Geography 17.1.54, translated by H. L. Jones, Loeb Classical Library 267, vol. VIII (1932), via LacusCurtius [S32, the source the entry itself cites]
audits.source_locator: Book XVII, chapter 1, section 54 (Loeb pp. 137-139), the Petronius-Candace war narrative on the fetched LacusCurtius chapter page (sections 25-54)
audits.source_excerpt: Among these fugitive were the generals of Queen Candacê, who was ruler of the Aethiopians in my time — a masculine sort of woman, and blind in one eye.
audits.retrieval_method: FetchURL retrieval of the public LacusCurtius chapter page (Loeb translation); section 54 located in the fetched text and quoted verbatim, including its printed archaic 'fugitive' and 'Candacê' with circumflex; copy of the fetched page saved by the FetchURL tool log, keywords indexed in scratch
audits.basis: The primary text verifies entry line 85 part by part: a ruling 'Candace' described as 'ruler of the Aethiopians in my time', her generals captured (commanders), her son at Napata (see source_excerpt_secondary), ambassadors offering to return captives and statues (see source_excerpt_ambassadors), in the war with Rome. The same passage also exhibits the gendered, disparaging portrait ('a masculine sort of woman, and blind in one eye') that entry line 86 requires to stay attributed to Strabo rather than serve as a neutral character sheet.
audits.coupling_implication: The layers stay separate as the entry's table demands: Strabo evidences a reigning queen through a foreign imperial report (reigning-queen evidence), not a Kushite self-description; the Meroitic title form `kdke` and its translation are separate philological questions carried by the tertiary corroboration; royal imagery in monuments is a distinct medium again. The passage's gendered description licenses attribution and design of foreign mishearing, not a universal warrior-queen caste or matriarchy.
audits.limits: The Loeb Jones translation is a mediated English rendering by a Roman-era author; the entry itself flags this perspective. The Meroitic title spelling (`kdke`/`ktke`), the nasal question, and the 'queen mother' contextualization were not verified from a linguistic edition - only through a tertiary page pointing to Hofmann 1981, p. 41 (see corroboration_kdke_forms_tertiary). Török 1997 pp. 213-214 (entry line 80 anchor) was not accessed. Labia 2018 does not use the word 'kandake' in the sections retrieved; it documents Amanishakheto's individual chronology and imagery instead (see corroboration_amanishakheto_chronology). No retrieved passage evidences or refutes a universal gender system; entry lines 87's calibration is a methodological absence-claim and was checked only for consistency with the sources, not proven by them. Partial support does not verify the entire compound claim.
